cl_meth_violence.short: In two long-term studies, violence was more common when people used meth. The cause is unclear.
cl_meth_violence.but: Both studies came from linked research teams, and neither could show which came first.
how: A review of mostly weak studies found the link shrank and became uncertain after other factors were counted.
In New Zealand, about 1,000 people followed from birth reported a bit more violence in times they used meth or speed.
In Australia, 469 people dependent on meth reported violent crime in 12 of 100 months with meth use and 3 of 100 without.
That study compared each person with themselves, but people reported use and crime for the same months.

cl_meth_siblings.short: Brothers and sisters never dependent on alcohol or drugs other than tobacco shared some brain differences with their sibling dependent on stimulants.
cl_meth_siblings.but: One study, and 94 in 100 of the dependent people were dependent on cocaine.
how: Brothers and sisters never dependent on alcohol or drugs other than tobacco shared some of the same brain differences as their sibling.
So some differences may run in families and come before drug use, but no one was scanned before they started.
More of these brothers and sisters smoked than the volunteers, and smoking was checked for only part of the scans.
94 in 100 of the dependent people were dependent on cocaine; the study does not mention meth.

cl_meth_violence._when: Use these if the relation stays insufficient evidence and the McKetin et al. (2020) anchors are added as qualifying.
cl_meth_violence.short: It is not settled whether meth use is linked to violence, once other things are counted.
cl_meth_violence.but: The studies could not show which came first, and most were weak.
how: A review of mostly weak studies found the link shrank and became uncertain after other factors were counted.
Two long-term studies, in New Zealand and Australia, found more violence in times of meth use.
In the Australian study of 469 people dependent on meth, violent crime came up in 12 of 100 months with use and 3 of 100 without.
The two studies share authors, and use and violence were reported for the same times.
